etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English crib, cribbe, from Old English crib, cryb, cribb, crybb (“couch, bed; manger, stall”), from Proto-West Germanic *kribbjā, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ (“crib, wickerwork”), from Proto-Indo-European *grebʰ-, *gerbʰ- (“bunch, bundle, tuft, clump”), from *ger- (“to turn, twist”).

Cognate with Saterland Frisian Kräbbe, Krääb, Krääf (“crib”), West Frisian krêbe (“crib”), Dutch krib (“crib, manger”), German Krippe (“rack, crib”), Danish krybbe (“crib”), Icelandic krubba (“crib”). Doublet of crèche. The sense of ‘stealing, taking notes, plagiarize’ seems to have developed out of the verb.

The criminal sense may derive from the 'basket' sense, circa the mid 18th century, in that a poacher could conceal poachings in such a basket (see the 1772 Samuel Foote quotation). The cheating sense probably derives from the criminal sense.

definitions.definition: (US) A baby’s bed with high, often slatted, often moveable sides, suitable for a child who has outgrown a cradle or bassinet.

quote.citation: 1889, Mark Twain, A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court:
quote.text: In two minutes I was kneeling by the child’s crib, and Sandy was dispatching servants here, there, and everywhere, all over the palace. I took in the situation almost at a glance -- membranous croup!

definitions.definition: (British) A bed for a child older than a baby.

quote.citation: 1847 October 16, Currer Bell [pseudonym; Charlotte Brontë], “[HTTPS://WEB.ARCHIVE.ORG/WEB/20140811201712/HTTP://ETEXT.VIRGINIA.EDU/ETCBIN/OT2WWW-PUBENG?SPECFILE=%2FTEXTS%2FENGLISH%2FMODSLAENG%2FPUBLICSEARCH%2FMODENGPUB.O2W CHAPTER ?]”, in Jane Eyre. An Autobiography. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London: Smith, Elder, and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: a day or two afterwards I learned that Miss Temple, on returning to her own room at dawn, had found me laid in the little crib; my face against Helen Burns’s shoulder, my arms round her neck. I was asleep, and Helen was -- dead.

definitions.definition: (nautical) A small sleeping berth in a packet ship or other small vessel
A wicker basket.
A manger, a feeding trough for animals elevated off the earth or floor, especially one for fodder such as hay.
The baby Jesus and the manger in a creche or nativity scene, consisting of statues of Mary, Joseph and various other characters such as the magi.
A bin for drying or storing grain, as with a corn crib.

quote.citation: 1835, Washington Irving, chapter 35, in A Tour on the Prairies:
quote.text: I began to think of my horse. He, however, like an old campaigner, had taken good care of himself. I found him paying assiduous attention to the crib of Indian corn, and dexterously drawing forth and munching the ears that protruded between the bars.

definitions.definition: A small room or covered structure, especially one of rough construction, used for storage or penning animals.

quote.citation: 1871, Richard Malcolm Johnston, Dukesborough Tales:
quote.text: A kitchen, a meat-house, a dairy, a crib with two stalls in the rear, one for the horse the other for the cow, were the out-buildings

quote.citation: 1611, “Proverbs 14:4”, in The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Where no oxen are, the crib is clean: but much increase is by the strength of the ox.

definitions.definition: A confined space, as with a cage or office-cubicle

quote.citation: 1846, Charles Dickens, Pictures from Italy:
quote.text: The singers were in a crib of wirework (like a large meat-safe or bird-cage) in one corner

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A job, a position; (British) an appointment.

quote.citation: 1904, Forrest Crissey, Tattlings of a Retired Politician:
quote.text: He had seen so many lean years of faithful service when the enemy held the corner on all the official cribs that, now in the days of his party’s fatness and of his own righteous reward, the habit of good, honest hustling stuck to him, and he lined up an array of pulls and indorsements that made him swell with happiness every time he went over the list.

quote.citation: 1893, Arthur Conan Doyle, The Adventure of the Stockbroker’s Clerk‎[1]:
quote.text: but if I have lost my crib and get nothing in exchange I shall feel what a soft Johnny I have been.

definitions.definition: A hovel, a roughly constructed building best suited to the shelter of animals but used for human habitation.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1599, William Shakespeare, Henry IV, Part 2, act 3, scene 1, lines 9–12:
quote.text: Why rather, sleep, liest thou in smoky cribs, / Upon uneasy pallets stretching thee, / And hushed with buzzing night-flies to thy slumber, / Than in the perfumed chambers of the great,

definitions.definition: A boxy structure traditionally built of heavy wooden timbers, to support an existing structure from below, as with a mineshaft or a building being raised off its foundation in preparation for being moved; see cribbing.
(usually in the plural) A collection of quotes or references for use in speaking, for assembling a written document, or as an aid to a project of some sort; a crib sheet.
(obsolete) A minor theft, extortion or embezzlement, with or without criminal intent.
(cribbage) The card game cribbage.

quote.citation: 1913, D[avid] H[erbert] Lawrence, “Chapter 12”, in Sons and Lovers, London: Duckworth & Co. […], →OCLC:
quote.text: “May we play crib, Mrs. Radford?” he asked.

definitions.definition: (cribbage) The cards discarded by players and used by the dealer.

quote.citation: 1814 May 9, [Jane Austen], chapter XI, in Mansfield Park: […], volume II, London:  […]  [George Sidney] for T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC, page 239:
quote.text: The cards were brought and Fanny played at cribbage with her aunt till bed-time; and as Sir Thomas was reading to himself, no sounds were heard in the room for the next two hours beyond the reckonings of the game—And that makes thirty-one, four in hand and eight in crib.

definitions.definition: (cryptography) A known piece of information corresponding to a section of encrypted text, that is then used to work out the remaining sections.
(southern New Zealand) A small holiday home, often near a beach and of simple construction.
(now chiefly Australia, New Zealand) A snack or packed lunch, especially as taken to work to eat during a break.

quote.citation: 2002, Alex Miller, Journey to the Stone Country, Allen & Unwin, published 2003, page 40:
quote.text: He ate a thick square of banana cake from his crib and stared into the fire.

definitions.definition: (Canada) A small raft made of timber.
(UK, obsolete, thieves' cant) The stomach.

quote.citation: 1641–42, Richard Brome, A Joviall Crew, or, The Merry Beggars‎[2], published 1652, act 2:
quote.text: Here's Pannum and Lap, and good Poplars of Yarrum, / To fill up the Crib, and to comfort the Quarron.

definitions.definition: A literal translation, usually of a work originally in Latin or Ancient Greek.

quote.citation: 1966, Millar MacLure, George Chapman: a critical study‎[3], page 171:
quote.text: [On Chapman's use of a Latin literal translation of Homer] As will appear, he blocked out his translation from the Latin crib, keeping one eye uneasily on the Greek, and, enlightened by Scapula or by his own poetic intuition, worked out his own rendering, often marking the departure from the Latin by a defiant note in the margin or commentary.

definitions.definition: (slang) A cheat sheet or past test used by students; crib sheet.
(slang, sometimes African-American Vernacular) One’s residence, house or dwelling place, or usual place of resort.

quote.citation: 1828, Edward Bulwer Lytton Baron Lytton, Pelham, Or, Adventures of a Gentleman:
quote.text: Why, you would not be boosing till lightman's in a square crib like mine, as if you were in a flash panny?

quote.citation: 1838, Charles Dickens, chapter XIX, in Oliver Twist:
quote.text: Toby and me were over the garden-wall the night afore last, sounding the panels of the door and shutters. The crib's barred up at night like a jail; but there's one part we can crack, safe and softly.

quote.citation: 2003, “In da Club”, in 50 Cent, Dr. Dre, Mike Elizondo (lyrics), Get Rich or Die Tryin', performed by 50 Cent:
quote.text: My flow, my show brought me the dough / That bought me all my fancy things / My crib, my cars, my pools, my jewels.

quote.citation: 2006, Noire [pseudonym], Thug-A-Licious: An Urban Erotic Tale, New York, N.Y.: One World, Ballantine Books, →ISBN, page 109:
quote.text: I knew every inch ofthis joint. I had come of age up in here, and it was more of a home to me than the crib where I rested my head each night.

quote.citation: 2013, Rockstar Games, Grand Theft Auto V, scene: Firing rockets in Franklin's house:
quote.text: Franklin Clinton (Shawn Fonteno): Eh stop shootin' rockets at my crib!"

definitions.definition: (transitive) To place or confine in a crib.

quote.citation: 1828, Thomas Keightley, The Fairy Mythology, volume I, London: William Harrison Ainsworth, page 223:
quote.text: They may go to their beds and give themselves no trouble about their work, and yet in the morning the maids will find the kitchen swept up, and water brought in, and the men will find the horses in the stable well cleaned and curried, and perhaps a supply corn cribbed for them from the neighbours barns.

definitions.definition: To shut up or confine in a narrow habitation; to cage; to cramp.

quote.citation: 1860, Isaac Taylor, “(please specify the page)”, in Ultimate Civilization and Other Essays, London: Bell and Daldy […], →OCLC:
quote.text: if only the vital energy be not cribbed or cramped

quote.citation: a. 1606, William Shakespeare, Macbeth, act 3, scene 4, lines 23–24:
quote.text: But now I am cabin'd, cribbed, confined, bound in, / To saucy doubts and fears

definitions.definition: (transitive) To collect one or more passages and/or references for use in a speech, written document or as an aid for some task; to create a crib sheet.
(transitive, informal) To plagiarize; to copy; to cheat.

quote.citation: 1857, Thomas Hughes, Tom Brown's School Days:
quote.text: He then proceeded to patch his tags together with the help of his Gradus, producing an incongruous and feeble result of eight elegiac lines, the minimum quantity for his form, and finishing up with two highly moral lines extra, making ten in all, which he cribbed entire from one of his books, beginning "O genus humanum," and which he himself must have used a dozen times before, whenever an unfortunate or wicked hero, of whatever nation or language under the sun, was the subject.

quote.citation: 2017 August 9, Laura Bradley, “How Star Wars: The Last Jedi Will—and Won’t—Echo The Empire Strikes Back”, in Vanity Fair‎[4]:
quote.text: This subplot—as well as a few other threads that have been teased from the Star Wars saga’s next installment—prompts another question: just how much of this film’s plot will be cribbed from The Empire Strikes Back?

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To install timber supports, as with cribbing.
(transitive, archaic) To steal or embezzle.

quote.citation: 1772, Samuel Foote, The Nabob‎[5], published 1778, act 1, page 22:
quote.text: There are a brace of birds and hare, that I cribbed this morning out of a basket of game.

quote.citation: 1848, Charles Dickens, “14”, in Dombey and Son:
quote.text: It was very easy, Briggs said, to make a galley-slave of a boy all the half-year, and then score him up idle; and to crib two dinners a-week out of his board, and then score him up greedy; but that wasn’t going to be submitted to, he believed, was it?

quote.citation: 1920 June, The Electrical Experimenter, New York, page 151, column 2:
quote.text: "Somebody crib the mayor's crown jools, or has some joyous cuss eloped with the auto patrol?"

definitions.definition: (India) To complain, to grumble

quote.citation: 1957, L.P.Hartley, chapter XI, in Hireling, page 90:
quote.text: She calls on the neighbours, she's out half the time and doesn't answer the telephone, and when I start cribbing she just laughs.

definitions.definition: To crowd together, or to be confined, as if in a crib or in narrow accommodations.

quote.citation: 1661, John Gauden, Anti Baal-Berith‎[6], page 35:
quote.text: […]  who ſought to make the glory of the Nation and Church of England, which was ever Regal and Epiſcopal ſince it was Chriſtian, truckle under a Scotch Canopy, and to make Biſhops to crib in a Presbyterian trundle-bed; as much as Kingly Majeſtie, to be confounded with Democracy.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of a horse) To seize the manger or other solid object with the teeth and draw in wind.
